newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Hongkong Bank gets first LAF.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Hongkong Bank gets first LAF.

text.p: Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corp brought the year's first Hong Kong dollar floating rate certificate of deposit issue to Asian debt markets on Wednesday.
The HK$2.0 billion issue is due in February 2002 and there are no puts or calls. It was priced at par to float at 30 basis points over the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate.
With fees, the all-in return to top-tier managers is 38 basis points. HSBC Markets arranged the deal.
Bankers were generally positive on the issue.
"The pricing is a little bit tight but not too tight. I might have preferred 39 or 40 basis points," said a syndicate manager at a European bank.
"But the issue is attractive because of the LAF (Liquidity Adjustment Facility) eligibility and because of the tax concession," he said.
Application has been made to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to accept the certificates as eligible for use at its Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), or discount window.
Eligibility for LAF tends to make an issue more attractive to banks because holders of the qualifying debt can engage in repurchase agreements with the monetary authority, increasing liquidity.

The certificates also are expected to qualify for a Hong Kong tax break that halves the levy on gains from debt instruments to 8.25 percent if they are issued in the territory and meet certain other requirements, such as a five-year tenor.
Standard Chartered Bank launched a similar transaction last July -- five-year paper that was LAF and tax-break eligible -- that paid an all-in of 40 basis points.
That paper is trading around 39 basis points now.
"At first glance, the deal seems reasonably priced. Hongkong Bank is a top bank and we will be looking at the issue positively," said a manager at a Japanese bank in Hong Kong.
"The pricing is not too kind, but it is not too tough either," he added.

Syndicate managers had mixed views on how enticing the LAF label is to bank lenders, with some citing the resilience of LAF issues in the secondary market and others saying LAF paper has lost some of its allure lately.
"Banks accumulated LAF paper last year in anticipation of Hong Kong's RTGS system as a way of putting in an insurance policy in the event of a crisis," said a manager at a U.S. bank.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority launched a Real Time Gross Settlement System for securities in early December.

But recently banks have been finding that their need for liquidity in the form of LAF and, more specifically, Hong Kong government paper, may be less than they anticipated last year, the U.S. banker said.

The HKMA's most recent auction of one-month Exchange Fund Bills was undersubscribed, a result the HKMA said was at least partially a result of banks' growing familiarity with their liquidity requirements under the RTGS system.
In other Hong Kong news, Dao Heng Bank is expected to set a subordinated bond issue of some US$180 million. Merrill Lynch is tipped to lead the issue.
